CT Entrepreneur Consortium · Federated Model Prototype · Aug 2026

The Federated Compact

Connecticut's entrepreneur support organizations each keep their own systems and their own client relationships — yet entrepreneurs retell their story at every door, referrals vanish into cold emails, and nobody can show the state what the ecosystem achieves together.

This is a working prototype of the federated answer: instead of everyone joining one central registry, each organization keeps its own software and data, and agrees to a small shared compact — a handful of common fields, consent rules the entrepreneur controls, and a way to recognize the same person across systems.

No new UI. No new platform. And the shared list is held in common — jointly governed, no single organization owns it.
Just a small protocol your existing systems already speak — five plain HTTPS calls:

▶ POST /partnerUpsertPerson …an agency's system talks… ◀ HTTP 201 { "ok": true, "action": "created" } …the network answers. The sandbox is online now. Nothing to install — any HTTP tool can call it.

Everything in this deck is running code, open source under MIT — github.com/jrlogan/Entrepreneurship-Nexus — and the live demo at the end runs against a sandbox you can call from your own laptop.

The heart of the compact · what everyone signs up to

Always shared · shared by consent · never shared

Always · by the compact

The operational minimum, visible to staff at orgs the entrepreneur actually works with:

  • Name and email (identity core)
  • Each org's own participation & referral records with them
  • Shared tags ("entrepreneur", "patent")
Only with their consent

Off by default; the entrepreneur opts in from an email link:

  • Listing in the cross-org network directory
  • Another org seeing a first org's records — asked per share, or granted upfront to named trusted partners
  • Revocable; data-deletion built in
Never shared

Stays inside the org that wrote it:

  • Internal record IDs (each org sees only its own)
  • Interaction notes (excluded even from webhooks)
  • Financials, custom fields — anything unmapped

Privacy Notice — the entrepreneur signs

"Each ESO only sees records they have created or that you have explicitly shared with them." · "We do not sell your data… notes are confidential between you and the recording organization."

Network Compact — the entrepreneur signs

"You are joining something shared by design." Five plain-language sections covering what becomes visible, that consent is required each time a new organization asks, that access is revocable, and that "organizations violating the compact can be removed from the network."

Data Usage Agreement — each org signs

"Access entrepreneur information solely to provide ecosystem support services." Versioned signatures, in-app; both documents are drafts this group edits before v1.0.

The mechanism in one picture

The life of one shared record

Adoption · value add, not extra work

What this asks of your organization

Pick a rung. Every level is optional, and level 0 is real participation.

LevelWhat you doWhat you get
0 · Nothing changesKeep using emailReferrals arrive with an ID; accept or decline from links in the email — no login, no form. Less work than today's follow-up forms.
1 · Refer through the networkStaff send referrals to a network address as they happenEach referral creates a tracked record for that one entrepreneur, and the consent email goes to them right then. The shared record set grows person by person, from real activity.
2 · Live syncYour system calls the API on saveThe five calls you just saw, firing as staff work. An integration playbook, OpenAPI spec, and an AI-assistant prompt that scaffolds the client code are included.
3 · SSO & webhooksRegister your OAuth server / an HTTPS endpoint"Sign in with [your org]" on the shared node; signed real-time events into your system.
What level 2 actually involves, step by step
  • Credentials — an org id and API key. One email; your key is yours alone and every write is attributable to you.
  • Map your fields — which of your columns is first name, email, venture name. About an hour. Your record IDs are never translated; they ride along as your external_ref.
  • Map your taxonomy — your program names onto the shared vocabulary.
  • Push on save — when staff save a record, your system fires the call. An afternoon; the AI prompt scaffolds it for your stack.
  • Grow organically — each entrepreneur enters the first time you actually work with them, and the consent email goes to them at that moment.
  • Later, optionally — webhooks for real-time referrals; register your login as an identity provider. Both reversible.

No bulk imports, at any level. Nobody hands over a database or a CSV. The network builds up organically — an entrepreneur enters it the first time an org actually works with them, and the shared agreement goes to that person at that moment.

Compatible with the centralized prototype: Entrepreneur Central's registry can plug in at level 3 as one identity provider among peers — a central front-door as a member of the network, not its owner.

The optional shared UI · try it: nexus-compact-demo.web.app

What the entrepreneur sees

Integration is the core. The interface is the optional layer — and the entrepreneur is the one person who actually needs it, because they're the only party who should see the whole ecosystem at once. For agencies it's a backup: a place to look at data, or a starting system for a small org that doesn't have one yet.

One founder, the whole ecosystem

Supporting ESOs, their venture, initiatives, and a cross-org activity feed — assembled from what each organization already records. The founder never assembles this by hand, and no single agency could show it to them.

Note the REDACTED rows

Activity is visible — an agency logged something, on this date — while the notes stay with the recording organization. That's the compact's privacy rule, enforced in the UI. Whether founders should see notes written about them is a compact decision, not a technical one.

The hard question · "we all spell names differently"

Identity, duplicates, and how they get fixed

Every data-sharing effort dies here. The answer is three separate jobs — avoid, resolve, reverse — and refusing to guess in the middle one.

  1. Avoid — match on things that don't vary Your own record ID first (external_ref), then exact email or domain. Never on spelling. "Bob Smith" vs "Robert Smith Jr." never auto-merges.
  2. Flag — a weak signal is a question, not a decision Similar name + same email domain? The system creates the record so nobody is blocked, and flags the pair for review. The API never silently merges two people.
  3. Resolve — a human decides, in the GUI This is what the interface is for: an admin sees both records side by side and picks the survivor. Most days the API does everything; the screen exists for exactly this.
  4. Reverse — every merge is undoable The merged record is archived and tombstoned, never deleted, recording precisely which IDs moved. Unmerge puts back exactly those and nothing else.

Why nobody loses their pointer

On merge, every partner's ID from the losing record is copied to the survivor and its lookup entry is repointed. An agency that only knows its own ID keeps resolving to the live record — no reconciliation on your side, no broken integration.

The safety properties

  • Merges run in a transaction — no half-merged state.
  • Tombstoned records redirect reads to the survivor.
  • Merge and unmerge are both written to the audit log, with who and when.
  • Only platform admins and ecosystem managers can merge.

Try it in the compact demo: Data Quality shows pending duplicates with a side-by-side review and a survivor choice.

Live demo · running now against the hosted sandbox

Two independent systems, one shared record

Two agencies, two API keys, no coordination between them — the terminal does the talking. Watch one field.

Provider A · Entrepreneurship Foundation

Keeps its own tracker. Contact #contact-4402 stays its own ID forever.

Provider B · IP Factory

Keeps its matching app. Member #member-118 stays its own ID forever.

# A registers her — A's own system, A's own form ▶ POST /partnerUpsertPerson key: EF's ◀ 201 { "nexus_id": "ZQWLB…", "action": "created" } # weeks later she walks into B — B pushes from its own CRM ▶ POST /partnerUpsertPerson key: IP Factory's ◀ 200 { "nexus_id": "ZQWLB…", "action": "linked" } ← same record # and B keeps working with A completely offline ▶ GET /partnerGetPerson?source=ipfactory_matching&id=member-118 ◀ 200 "external_refs": [ { "source": "ipfactory_matching" } ] ← only B's own ref. A's contact-4402 is never disclosed.

One identity, no duplicate

Same email → same shared record, and the two agencies never contacted each other. No central signup form; she registered once, at the org she actually visited.

No single point of failure

Nothing in that last call touched Agency A — it can be down entirely. Logins behave the same way: sessions are minted independently, so an entrepreneur still gets in when their home org is offline.

Your turn · the sandbox is live right now

Try it from your laptop — nothing to install

# paste into any terminal — edit only the two PASTE_ placeholders: BASE=https://us-central1-entrepreneurship-nexus-staging.cloudfunctions.net curl -s -X POST $BASE/partnerUpsertPerson \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "X-Nexus-API-Key: PASTE_YOUR_KEY" \ -d '{"external_ref":{"source":"my_crm","id":"1"}, "ecosystem_id":"eco_connecticut", "eso_org_id":"PASTE_YOUR_ORG", "first_name":"Test","last_name":"Person", "email":"test@example.com"}'
expected reply: { "ok": true, "action": "created" }

  • Hand it to your AI — increasingly the fastest path. Two ready-made prompts, written to be pasted straight into Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or Copilot:

Get your own key — one call, once you have the code

Ask me for the sandbox invite code — it isn't in the repo, because the repo is public and a published gate code is no gate at all. Then:

curl -s -X POST $BASE/provisionDemoAgency -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"name":"Your Org Name","invite_code":"THE CODE"}'

Returns your demo org id + a fresh API key (shown once). Keys are org-scoped: everything you write is attributable to you, and only you see your own IDs.

The two-person trick

Pair up. Both push the same email from your two different orgs. The second push comes back "action": "linked" — you just federated.

Sandbox etiquette: made-up people only, no real client data; everything is purged periodically. Full quickstart with expected responses: docs/partner-api/TRY_IT.md in the repo.

Discussion · the group's to-do list

What the group must decide — in order

  1. Ratify the compact — the governance principles: sovereignty, consent, permitted uses.
    Draft starting point — three signed documents, already written

    Network Compact (entrepreneur-facing, 5 sections): "You are joining something shared by design" · "What becomes visible across organizations" · "You stay in control of what moves" · "Why this is better than a central database" · "What this organization will not do."

    Data Usage Agreement (staff-facing, 6 sections): permitted uses · confidentiality obligations · prohibited activities · audit and accountability · reporting obligations · consequences of violation.

    Privacy Notice (entrepreneur-facing, 5 sections): what is stored · who can see it · cross-org sharing · your rights · what we do not do.

    Sample language, verbatim: "No single organization holds everyone's data… we agree on shared standards so your information can move between organizations with your permission rather than being duplicated or locked behind one system." and "Organizations violating the compact can be removed from the network."

    Read all three drafts in full →

    Open question: does the compact bind organizations, or individuals at them — and who enforces removal?

  2. Fix the common core fields — the small set every org shares.
    Draft starting point — data-standards v1.0

    Person: first_name, last_name, email, external_ref (+ optional tags)
    Organization: name, description, roles (+ optional tax status, NAICS, url)
    Participation: type, status, name, start_date

    Open question: is anything here too much to ask — or missing?

  3. Pick the operator — who runs the shared node.
    Four scenarios, from the group's own thread
    • State-run — funding, but entrepreneur reluctance and election-cycle risk.
    • A lead nonprofit — one NGO as system administrator, bound not to exploit the data.
    • Joint council — one seat per adopting organization; hires the host.
    • Marketplace — each org self-hosts and bridges; best service wins.

    MIT licensing keeps every option open — and reversible.

  4. Run a pilot — prove it with real referrals before committing.
    Proposed shape

    Two organizations integrate against the sandbox; real referrals flow for 30 days; the group reviews what worked at the next meeting. Keys, playbook, and OpenAPI spec are ready today.

    Open question: which two orgs, and who is each one's technical contact?

Four more on the list — taxonomy, agreement text, identity, metrics
  • Agree the shared taxonomy — participation types, referral statuses, tags.
    Open question: this is deliberately generous — you map your terms onto it once and keep your own internally. What's missing, and what would you never collect?
  • Set the entrepreneur agreement text — the consent language every org presents.
    Open question: should founders see notes written about them?
  • Choose the identity approach — which orgs offer sign-in; how the rest link.
    Open question: who is allowed to assert an identity for the network?
  • Define the shared metrics — what we report to the state.
    Open question: which numbers does the state actually reward — and who publishes them?

Before the demo · how to read what you'll see

Every step is one question and one answer

Wherever you see this format, it's a real exchange with the live sandbox: a message sent and the reply received — the same way your CRM or website would do it, invisibly, in a fraction of a second. Nothing to download: any HTTP tool (curl, Postman, the browser-based Hoppscotch) speaks it, and sandbox keys are available today — ask me for the invite code.

▶ POST /partnerUpsertPerson ↑ the question: "here's a person from my records — add or update them." Sent over the web (HTTPS), like submitting a form X-Nexus-API-Key: nxk_…EF ↑ the sender's badge — proves WHICH org is asking, and scopes what they're allowed to see ◀ HTTP 201 { "ok": true, "action": "created" } ↑ the reply: "done" (201 = created something new), plus what happened, in plain terms
▶ outgoing

A system asks

An organization's existing software sends a small package of text (JSON) to the shared network node. Nobody types this by hand — it fires automatically when staff save a record.

◀ incoming

The network answers

The reply always says whether it worked and what happened. The numbers are just status shorthand: 200/201 = success, 401/403 = wrong badge, 404 = not found.

action

The word to watch

"created" = new shared record · "updated" = same record refreshed · "linked" = the network recognized an entrepreneur two orgs both know — the whole point of the demo.

The assignment · agreed Aug 7

Two prototypes, one spec

Chris built the centralized model — a shared registry that owns entrepreneur identity. This is the federated answer to the same four steps: every organization keeps its own system, its own data, its own IDs.

  1. A new user registers as an entrepreneur …in a provider's own system — no central signup form
  2. The entrepreneur is linked to service provider A …a dated, typed relationship on the shared record
  3. They link to a second provider B …B's system recognizes the same person: action: "linked"
  4. The entrepreneur works with B while A is offline …no single point of failure, in data or login

Step 2 & 3 up close · the real work is agreement, not code

Mapping keys and taxonomy

The "FirstName vs First Name" problem, solved once per organization: a short mapping from your schema onto the compact's small shared core. Example — Entrepreneurship Foundation's tracker:

Key structures
EF trackerCompact field
Member_FNamefirst_name
Member_Emailemail
MemberID 4402external_ref.id ← stays yours, untranslated
Venture_Nameorganization.name
Notes, financials, 40 other columnsnot mapped — never leave your system
Taxonomy
EF's termsShared vocabulary
Business Plan Competition '26type: program · status: active
Mentor pairingtype: service
Alum (2019 cohort)type: program · status: past
"Seeking investment" flagtags: ["seeking_funding"]

The shared vocabulary is deliberately generous, not minimal — 17 versioned vocabularies covering participation, referral outcomes, venture stage, support needs, outcome metrics, owner characteristics, and certifications. Being expansive costs an organization nothing: you map your terms onto it once and keep your own internally. What you can't map, you simply don't send. Ratifying the list is a consortium decision, which is exactly why it's on the agenda.

The email path, for real · zero integration required

A referral, start to close, without anyone logging in

What the receiving org gets

A real email — generated by the running system — carrying the venture, stage, support needs, and the referrer's own introduction notes. Then three one-click buttons: Review Referral, Accept Referral, Mark as Complete.

"These one-click buttons work for 7 days and can only be used once." Signed, expiring links — so closing the loop takes a click, not an account.

And the loop actually closes
  • The sender gets a receipt — their referral is logged and trackable.
  • The receiver gets this intake notice; accept or complete without logging in.
  • A follow-up notice chases the outcome — the step FORGE-style feedback forms ask humans to remember.

Every click updates the same shared referral record, so the status is visible to both sides and counts toward the ecosystem statistics.

Captured from real notices generated by the referral flow in test — not mockups.

Day to day · the two actions that build the timeline

How a referral happens · how a session gets logged

Sessions & milestones — logged where staff already work

Facts on the timeline, details at home

  • Coaching / mentoring: staff log the meeting in their own CRM as they do today; the system pushes a dated event — type, date, org. Notes never leave the recording org; sharing "it happened" is a per-event choice.
  • Memberships & programs: starts, completions, and lapses flow automatically (active → past, history kept). Outcomes (jobs, revenue) recorded as standard metrics, self-reported or verified.
The day-to-day payoff

Coordinate, don't duplicate

  • Before reaching out about a shared client, staff see who's already helping and how recently — and can call that agency to coordinate.
  • Start at the email level today; integrate later. Every level feeds the same timeline — and the statistics — with no extra reporting work.

The hub · what operators see when the API is doing the work

Running the network, not just connecting to it

Day to day the API does everything. The console is where the humans running the network see whether it's actually healthy — and it shows each person only what their role allows.

Network operator's view
  • Connection health — each partner integration with status, records synced, and last-sync time.
  • Duplicate queue — pending conflicts waiting on a human, one click to review.
  • Keys — issue and revoke per organization; every write stays attributable.
  • Webhooks & delivery log — what fired, where it went, and a simulator to test an endpoint before going live.
  • Sent mail — the log of notices the system has actually sent, so "did they get it?" has an answer.
Partner representative's view

The same console, scoped by role. An ESO admin sees their own organization's keys, webhooks, and tooling — and the console says so plainly:

"Cross-organization sync status is hidden for ESO admins. This workspace is limited to your organization's API keys, webhooks, and integration tooling."

Sovereignty isn't only a promise in the compact — it's what each account can actually see.

The statistics payoff · aggregate & anonymous, by design

What the shared timeline can answer

For the state & funders
  • Entrepreneurs served statewide — deduplicated. Linked identity means a founder helped by four orgs counts once, not four times. That's what makes the number credible.
  • Businesses started, and still operating at 1 / 5 / 10 years — the survival-rate study EF assembled by hand via LinkedIn becomes a query, with national baselines for comparison.
  • Jobs (FT/PT) and revenue — standard metrics, each tagged self_reported or verified, aggregated for the funding case.
  • Retention in Connecticut — where network-supported ventures end up.
For the network & each org
  • Referral flow that closes: volume, acceptance rate, and time-to-first-meeting — by org pair, so bottlenecks are visible.
  • Collaboration measured: how many entrepreneurs are served by 2+ organizations, and which hand-offs actually happen.
  • Program reach: enrollments, completions, and coaching cadence across the ecosystem.
  • Your own view: each org sees its clients' cross-org activity — support better, or call the other agency to coordinate.

All of it is aggregate and anonymous — entrepreneur-level data never leaves the consent rules to produce a statistic. And none of it is extra reporting work: the numbers are a byproduct of referrals, enrollments, and sessions the orgs already record.
